title: Yemen Army Launches Hundreds of Strikes on Houthis, Claims 700 Killed – Al Jazeera Report
body:
The Yemeni army announced on Tuesday that it had intensified air and artillery strikes across Houthi‑controlled territories, claiming more than 700 enemy combatants were killed in a series of operations that also sealed a vital mountain crossing linking the rebel‑held town of al‑Houban with the government‑controlled city of Taiz. The offensive, which has seen hundreds of sorties over the past week, marks the latest escalation in a conflict that has already devastated the country’s most densely populated regions and pushed the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse.  

The newly secured crossing, situated on the strategic road that runs through the rugged highlands of western Yemen, had been a lifeline for Houthi supply convoys moving between their stronghold in the north and the front lines around Taiz. By cutting this artery, government forces aim to isolate rebel units, restrict the flow of weapons and ammunition, and pressure the Houthis into negotiations. Military officials said the operation involved coordinated air strikes, artillery bombardments and ground troops who seized key high‑ground positions before establishing defensive outposts.  

While the army’s figures of 700 Houthi fighters killed have not been independently verified, they underscore a pattern of heavy‑handed tactics that have become commonplace since the conflict entered its fifth year. The Yemeni capital, Sanaa, has been repeatedly targeted in a campaign described by officials as “precision strikes” aimed at degrading the rebels’ command and control infrastructure. Satellite imagery released by the United Nations corroborates the presence of extensive damage to several government buildings and residential districts in the capital, raising concerns about civilian casualties and the potential for further displacement.  

The surge in hostilities comes amid a fragile cease‑fire that was brokered earlier this year by the United Nations and Saudi Arabia, which has largely held in the south but remains tenuous in the north. Analysts warn that the latest round of attacks could unravel the limited progress made toward a political settlement. “Every time a strategic node like the al‑Houban‑Taiz corridor is contested, it not only reshapes the battlefield but also tests the resolve of the diplomatic community,” said Dr. Lina Al‑Saadi, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “The government’s push to isolate the Houthis may yield short‑term military gains, but it risks inflaming local grievances and complicating humanitarian access.”  

Humanitarian agencies have already reported a sharp increase in the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) fleeing the intensified fighting in the highlands. The United Nations World Food Programme warned that supply routes into Taiz, which relies heavily on aid convoys, could be jeopardised if the crossing remains under government control. Meanwhile, the International Committee of the Red Cross has called for an immediate cease‑fire to allow safe passage for medical teams and to prevent further civilian casualties.  

Looking ahead, the trajectory of the conflict will likely hinge on whether the Yemeni government can sustain its offensive without alienating the already war‑wearied population, and whether the Houthis can regroup and launch counter‑offensives from their remaining strongholds. International stakeholders, including the United Nations and regional powers, are expected to intensify diplomatic pressure in the coming weeks, urging both sides to return to the negotiating table before the fighting spreads to additional civilian corridors. The coming days will be critical in determining whether the recent gains translate into a broader pathway toward peace or simply fuel another cycle of violence in a country already ravaged by years of war.
